Levenson combines rivalries, religion, technology, illness, money and even hanging chads into a bubbling jumble of guilt, jealousy, remembrance and soap opera, resulting in a juicy melting pot of drama, comedy and realistic family strife.
If I Forget succeeds both as a thoughtful family drama filled with wit and as a compelling dissection of the world we live in.

But rare is the opportunity to quietly take in all sides of so many emotionally fraught subjects through such witty, articulate, and impassioned voices as Levenson has created for this world premiere with Roundabout Theatre Company.
It's a deeply absorbing, issues-oriented family drama that's likely to hit a nerve in both head and heart.

"If I Forget”, by Steven Levenson, slightly dragging in the beginning, is a great family drama that unfolds against the backdrop of broader political issues.
An engaging play for open-minded theatergoers.
Despite its flaws, Levenson’s depiction of recognizable and articulate family dealing with issues in an impassioned way makes for an engaging evening in the theatre.
Levenson forces audiences to confront what are, for many, long- and strongly-held beliefs, stances that have cemented as a matter of fact without critical thinking or questioning.

This new work is in many ways the better play; unlike Bad Jews, it feels less like a mouthpiece for the playwright’s opinion, and the payoff for a very long run-time is that you have time to develop sympathy for (almost) every character.
The problem with If I Forget, is it crashes and burns to a strange halt.
